subtopic: MR. SPEAKER  STATEMENT ON QUESTION RAISED BY MEMBER FOR GREY-BRUCE
MR. SPEAKER  STATEMENT ON QUESTION RAISED BY MEMBER FOR GREY-BRUCE
speechtext:
On October 17, in the course of proceedings, the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) rising on a question of privilege stated in part as follows:
Yesterday-
That was Wednesday, October 16.
-a motion for the production of papers was on the order paper, motion No. 99, and there was an extended discussion with regard to the existence of a certain document. In the course of that discussion it was stated by the Postmaster General that this document did not exist. These words are to be found in Hansard at page 3626. A little earlier the Secretary of State also stated that the document did not exist. This was in accord with discussions which took place during consultation between the Secretary of State and the Post Office Department.
For the benefit of the house and the country, I have such a document before me now. As a matter of fact it is a copy of the document in question the production of which was requested under the terms of motion No. 99. If the house so desires I am prepared to table it, and that would end the discussion.
Later the hon. gentleman went on to say:
If I may say a further word, the main point at this juncture is not whether the list which I have is authentic, though I believe it to be so. It is that the Secretary of State misled the house yesterday when he said this particular document did not exist. Also, if the words of the Secretary of State were clear, and I believe they were, then of course the Postmaster General had misled the Secretary of State as he misled the entire house.
As the hon. gentleman implied, there were two points involved in this question. If the house will permit, I would like to deal first with the question of whether a private member may table a document. Citation 209, Beauchesne's fourth edition, states in part: Papers are laid before the house in pursuance of
(1)	Provisions of an act of parliament:
(2)	An order of the house;
(3)	An address to the crown;
(4)	The command of the crown;
(5)	Standing orders of the house.
According to this citation no member can table a document, as in the present circumstances, unless there is some authority for such action. I think the hon. gentleman from Grey-Bruce tacitly admitted this fact when he asked for unanimous consent to table the document.
The second point raised by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce is that the hon. Postmaster General as well as the Secretary of State misled the house when they stated that such a document did not exist. I must say that after looking over the record the difficulty would appear to be a difference of opinion. On the one hand it is asserted that no such document had been prepared and does not exist, while on the other hand the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has a document which he contends is a copy thereof. In other words there is a dispute as to facts.
In this regard I would like to refer to citation 113, Beauchesne's fourth edition, where it is stated in part as follows:
-a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
Therefore in my opinion a prima facie breach of privilege does not arise in this instance.

subtopic: HAINES ROAD-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MAIN- TENANCE DURING WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether before the orders of the day are called I might have the permission of the house to revert to motions just to make a brief announcement. On a number of occasions questions have been raised in the house with regard to the Haines road, and for this reason I should now like to make a short statement on this subject.
The government has today decided not to close the Haines road this winter, subject of course to satisfactory negotiations in respect of the technical requirements necessary to effect such a policy. Keeping open the road during the winter months will be in the nature of a trial for one year to determine the

Inquiries of the Ministry feasibility of maintaining this road on a year round basis. The project will involve the co-operation not only of several government departments, including the Departments of Northern Affairs, Public Works and National Defence, but it will also require negotiation with the government of the United States.

subtopic: HAINES ROAD-ANNOUNCEMENT OF MAIN- TENANCE DURING WINTER

Mr. Speaker, may I just reply very briefly. I thank the minister for his announcement and for the decision which has been made to keep the Haines road open. His announcement will be welcomed most heartily by the people in the Yukon, I am sure, by the people in Alaska, and in fact all up and down the Pacific northwest coast where there is now, as he knows, a very successful ferry system in operation.
I hope the experiment leads to a decision by the department to keep the road open on a permanent basis. I am sure the minister and his colleagues in the government will find that it will be economically feasible and will introduce an economic viability in that part of the country and in Alaska which does not now exist.
I thank the minister very much for his consideration, also the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I should like to ask the minister why the Canadian delegation voted yesterday against the admission of mainland China to the United Nations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the draft resolution which was introduced this year was sponsored by Albania and not, as usual, by the Soviet union. While the Soviet union and

India, which have at various times in the past taken the lead in trying to secure a change in Chinese representation, promised to vote in favour of the draft resolution and indeed did so, it is notable that they did not sponsor the resolution this year.
The draft resolution which was presented provided for two things, the seating of representatives from communist China and the expulsion of representatives from the nationalist Chinese government. As Canadian representatives have said in recent years, the Canadian government is ready to consider carefully any proposal to settle equitably the question of Chinese representation; but an equitable solution, among other factors, must preserve for the people of Formosa the right to self determination. This year's resolution did not make such provision; therefore the Canadian delegation could not and did not support it. I believe the vote demonstrated that the majority of the United Nations member states shared the point of view of the government of Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: A supplementary question. Could I ask the minister why the Canadian delegation did not move an amendment providing for the seating of mainland China and also for representation in the United Nations for Formosa?

subtopic: CANADIAN VOTE ON ADMISSION OF COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the answer must be clear to my hon. friend. The reason the delegation did not is that it did not receive instructions accordingly from the government of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to resume the debate which started yesterday perhaps it is in order to summarize briefly what took place. We in the official opposition were lectured by the government for even suggesting that a want of confidence motion should be moved on this very vital issue concerning the economy of Canada today. We were told that the amendment was frivolous. The Prime Minister laughed at the issue.
Certainly we in the opposition did not necessarily ask for a supply motion yesterday and today. We were told we were going to have supply motions every week until, as is customary under the rules of the house, six supply motions had been brought forward. I was somewhat shocked by the attitude taken by the government house leader, the Prime Minister and the members who spoke for that party. We were lectured with regard to wasting the time of the house for two days. They wanted to get on with government business, but at the same time they ruled that we should have a supply motion.
I have listened to a great deal of debate since the recess. We were told that one of the prime purposes in calling us back on September 30 last was to settle the great lakes dispute. The government wanted to bring in legislation, and we in the opposition aided them on numerous occasions by unanimously agreeing with the house leader that the rules be set aside and debate proceeded with. I think more rules have been set aside by unanimous consent in the past three weeks in order to proceed with government items than in any similar period of parliamentary history.
To me the biggest waste of time in the house has been this continual haranguing over the seating of members, and I am glad to see that at last this matter has been settled, though perhaps not to the liking of all hon. members. But it should have been settled before we reconvened, and we have wasted two weeks. Now it is settled I hope we can get on with government legislation expeditiously so that all the measures the government wish to bring forward can be proclaimed and their results felt across the nation.
It amazes me, Mr. Speaker, to think that yesterday 2,000 members of a Canadian union-whether we like the S.I.U. does not really matter-came to parliament but went away unseen by the Prime Minister and unrecognized, as far as I know, by the government. We see in today's Ottawa Journal that
the Minister of Labour said "Return to Montreal, Mr. Banks, and then I will see you".
I can remember a few years ago, when western Canada was greatly concerned over possible government action, that 1,100 farmers came to Ottawa. The government of that day welcomed them, and the prime minister spoke to them and told them that he was aware of their problems. But what did we see yesterday? Perhaps I am a poor one to speak on behalf of a trade union, but yesterday we saw a complete disregard for our fellow men. We saw these S.I.U. members being badgered by individual backbenchers, but no official recognition was given them by the Prime Minister and they received no official acceptance or hearing by the government of the day. To me it was a shocking display of arrogance and indifference, of treating it as a laughing matter, as evidenced in the house last evening in particular. I do not want to go into details; I am sure all hon. members were aware of what happened on the hill yesterday.
Much has been said, Mr. Speaker, about United States interference. I for one am pleased to see that at last action is being taken with regard to the situation on the great lakes, action which I regret was not taken long before. I also regret that a voluntary agreement was not achieved. As I understand it, this public trusteeship will have jurisdiction over Canadian ships. Whenever an attempt was made to get a voluntary agreement, control was also wanted over United States interests on the great lakes. The public trusteeship will not have such control, and it is interesting to note that we have been given no assurance by the Prime Minister that the United States unions, through the President, have assured Canada that they will co-operate.
I think this matter is well detailed in today's Gazette. An article on the editorial page says this:
But proclaiming the trusteeship is only the first step.
The minister himself admitted that the worst is yet to come. As a western farmer I realize the position with which western Canada is faced. We have had one of the greatest crops and one of the greatest sales of wheat ever made, but we have had no co-operation from the government and a particular segment of the country in the settlement of a dispute which has raged since July. The Gazette continues:
The next step will be to deal with whatever defiance of the law may now be raised by the S.I.U. In this struggle, however, the government will have many resources of law and power: the resources, in fact, of the Canadian nation.

Labour Relations
But then looms the still larger question. What happens if the government of Canada finds itself confronted, not simply with one strategically powerful union in Canada, but with the force of the massive labour federation of the United States-the A.F.L.-C.I.O.?
I hope when the minister speaks this afternoon he will give us an assurance that Mr. Meany and the labour unions of the United States have agreed to co-operate with the public trusteeship, because we do want shipping on the great lakes to return to normal operation for the remaining part of the season.
The Montreal Gazette continues in this way:
Hope now must be placed in the law-the law whether in Canada or in the United States. Mr. Justice Norris, in his report on the Canadian maritime unions, pointed out that the supreme court of the United States-last February declared the principle that even when a ship of foreign registry is in the waters of the United States its domestic jurisdiction must be respected in domestic affairs, which includes labour relations.
This was the point I tried to make earlier today. In his many telephone conversations with the President, has the Prime Minister been given the assurance that the law will be enforced? Apparently not. Some hon. members yesterday asked the Prime Minister about telephone conversations he had had with the President. What did the President say?

speechtext: "Sorry, wrong number".

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
We had to interject two or three times to ask this, and the Prime Minister referred to it as an asinine interjection, as a stupid interruption; and he said, in a sense "You western members quit making these statements and don't bother me. I was talking to the President about something other than shipping on the great lakes", or that is what we were led to believe.
This is certainly not the stand western Canada would like to see taken by the government on this question. We are worried. We do not want the worst which is yet to come, as the Minister of Labour said. We want this matter settled by agreement among the parties-the shipping companies, the unions, the members and the men who do the work-so that exports of grain can move forward freely along the seaway.
I have heard many hon. members condemn Hal Banks, the leader of the S.I.U., and certainly I hold no love for him. Few hon. members have ever stood up and proclaimed him a great union leader. Even the New Democratic party members say he should be thrown out of Canada. I read from time to time of certain alien citizens who are deported from the United States. Why cannot we, on the evidence of the Norris report, now deport Hal Banks? This evidence has been available to the present government

since last July and the Minister of Justice has been prodded several times to take action in this regard. On page 296 of the Norris report this statement appears:
Banks obtained his absolute control in his union through the misuse of union funds, the hiring halls, the D.N.S. and R.O.C. cards, and the welfare plan. This has been fully established.
This evidence is fully set out in the Norris report which was tabled in this house last July. Why has the Minister of Justice not taken some action with regard to this man who is doing so much to corrupt relations and disrupt shipping on the great lakes? The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is perhaps the only hon. member who has a particular affection for him. Maybe he should have, and maybe he should not have, but surely he could read the evidence and if the evidence is clear, as Mr. Justice Norris has suggested it is, he should be prepared to bring in the necessary legislation to deport him. Similar action is taken in countries other than Canada. I think it is time we were the power of the land, as is suggested in today's Gazette. This government is the power of the land and should take action against any undesirable alien as is the case in this instance.
With regard to the shipping situation on the great lakes, we have been given no assurance that the lawlessness which is now going on will cease. From time to time I have tried to get an assurance from the government that they expect the co-operation of the Canadian unions, of the United States government and of the labour unions of the United States in enforcing the law. But the government cannot even give us an assurance that they will have the co-operation of the unions in Canada in carrying out this public trusteeship measure. The Minister of Labour refuses to see one of the trade union heads. This is no way to go about getting the co-operation of the unions in order that the trusteeship can operate with the good will of all concerned.
From time to time we have heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce defend his department and his own actions with regard to wheat sales. This whole discussion centres on wheat sales to a great extent, because more than half the freight shipped on the great lakes or through the St. Lawrence seaway is western grain. This is why we who come from western Canada are so concerned with shipping on the lakes. From time to time the minister has said that shipments will continue to move out, that there is no real problem.
I wish to remind the house that we have seen disclosures in United States newspapers of Canadian wheat board transactions. We

have asked for information and been unable to get it, but all we have to do is to read the United States newspapers. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked whether he would tell the United States government that these disclosures about Canadian wheat board contracts were not appreciated by the Canadian government, and that they could possibly harm wheat board sales on behalf of the farmers of western Canada. The minister told us he did not think this was necessary; the message would be got across, but he did not want to take any formal note of it because he was afraid to hurt their feelings down there. He did not want to give the impression that the Canadian and United States governments were at odds about anything, though the evidence is abundant that they are.
We are concerned about the possible effect of this shipping situation on wheat shipments to Russia. I read in a United States newspaper that there is a clause in the contract with Russia which permits the Russians to stop taking Canadian wheat and shift their order to the United States if the commitments are not met, if there is a strike or a stoppage of movement on the great lakes. This explains the concern I feel about this problem. We are committed to selling this wheat. Now the fight is to maintain deliveries. We are in danger of losing this order because of delayed action, slow action and perhaps even meaningless action, if the co-operation of the various unions cannot be maintained.
We hear requests from time to time that the quotas on western farms should be raised. It is evident they are far below last year's levels. As a result of the abundant wheat crop many farmers have grain in open bins in the fields. They want to get it into the elevators, into shelter, before winter sets in. They want the quotas opened up, but with the continual stumbling and fumbling which has gone on with regard to the shipping situation how can they look forward with optimism toward a solution of their storage problems? The shipping difficulties on the lakes are not yet settled and they may not be settled, despite this trusteeship arrangement. We read in the Financial Post that President Kennedy is greatly concerned about an election next year. He does not want to offend the unions in the United States.
There is another thought which enters my mind in this connection. President Kennedy is not too popular in the midwestern states. He is not too popular in the grain belt there. Perhaps if, by hook or by crook, in co-operation with Mr. Meany and the unions in the United States he could increase United States wheat sales to Russia it would
Labour Relations
strengthen his hand in the election next year in those states where he is not too popular. These are the fears which arise in my mind as a representative from western Canada.
We were told that President Kennedy and the Prime Minister were as close as peas in a pod. We were told they could get along and solve such problems as this. But we cannot even be given an assurance by the acting prime minister today that the President has said the law of the land will be enforced. During the summer a Canadian ship tied up in the port of Chicago. It could not be loaded. A court injunction was obtained, and the fine for refusing to load was supposed to be $3,000 a day. Still the ship was not loaded, and eventually it had to leave the port and move into Canadian waters. This is what we fear for the future. We want some guarantee from this government that our shipping will not find itself once again faced with such circumstances.
Some time ago the Minister of Finance warned that if we were not extremely careful we would lose control of our own country. Well, there has not been much evidence in the last two months that we really have control over our own affairs or that we are masters of our own house. If this trend continues we will certainly be in danger of losing our sovereignty. We all hope that after the trusteeship bill has been proclaimed some sort of co-operation can be developed between this country and the United States. Only a few months ago the former government was ostracized as being anti-American. We were told that a Liberal government would get the co-operation of the United States.
We want to see some evidence that hon. gentlemen opposite are now getting this cooperation. Up to the present, in its dealings with important questions involving shipping, labour, and the wheat trade, there has been no evidence of this co-operation, and western Canada stands to suffer most from the lawlessness which has been permitted to continue on the great lakes.
We in western Canada have been laughed at in Ottawa whenever we have mentioned wheat. There have been times when we have mentioned it too often. We have been called dirty dogs by members of the present government. However, we still believe it is our duty to rise at every opportunity and point out the problems as they appear to us, in the hope that the government will take the advice of the opposition and introduce certain measures to alleviate those problems.
In so far as this problem is concerned, we have been given a great deal of hope because we note, in looking over the record of the

Labour Relations
present government, that they introduced a series of ideas on the budget, but the opposition and others outside the house convinced the government that many of these measures should not be implemented. We convinced the government they would not work. Many of these provisions have been dropped, and some of the taxes have been reduced. This gives the opposition some hope that we can successfully urge the government to take action to proclaim this trusteeship and get assurance from the United States government that they will co-operate. We should like the United States government to get the assurance of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. that they, too, will co-operate. I would strongly suggest that when the trusteeship is set up, the trustees take steps to ensure that great lakes personnel will be given the freedom to join whatever union they desire. The trustees should make sure that the unions operate free and democratic hiring halls.
I think it was evident during the longshoremen strike that there should be some assurance given that free, secret elections will be held in these unions. The leaders of the longshoremen's union said, no, we won't accept the settlement; but when a secret vote was taken the result was something like four to one in favour of accepting the terms of the shipping companies, and the longshoremen went back to work. I urge the public trustees to make sure they maintain secret elections in all cases in which union officials and union matters are concerned. I feel that there is plenty of evidence in the Norris report indicating the need for a private audit of union pension funds and other union funds. Certainly, I should like to see the public trustees establish principles in the years ahead to ensure that these matters will be looked after properly and accurately for the benefit of union members.
I think perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I have given you and the government some of my views concerning the operation of shipping on the St. Lawrence seaway. I hope, along with all Canadians, that the act will be proclaimed and that shipping will return to normal as soon as possible. I hope, too, that we will have the co-operation of the United States government and the United States unions in solving this grave problem affecting all of Canada, and particularly western Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject that has been raised in this supply amendment relates to a problem which has accumulated over a long period of time. Thus, it is the accumulated product developed over quite a number of years that is now being dealt with by the Department of Labour. It is my view that because of its

history it ought to be regarded as a shared burden, a shared responsibility, because if one examines the background of this problem, he will find that there are quite a number of groups who ought to accept their share of responsibility for the kind of difficulty that reached its most colourful manifestation on parliament hill yesterday.
I am thankful, Mr. Speaker, for the support that has been accorded the policy of the government by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). I appreciate that they have realized the difficulties of this problem. It is not as easy as has been implied by members of the official opposition to deal with it in an effective manner.
In introducing the legislation preparatory to setting up the trusteeship, I mentioned in the house that the situation would likely get worse before it got better. This statement has been borne out by the events of yesterday and by the events of last Friday. On Friday last, the rights committee of the seafarers international union issued a directive asking all members of the seafarers union to leave their ships to stage a march in demonstration on parliament hill. These instructions suggested that this demonstration was to be a peaceful and responsible representation to members of parliament. Surely no members of parliament have any objection to citizens of this country coming to parliament hill and giving some expression of their views to members of parliament. Surely also, Mr. Speaker, such demonstrations if they are held must be lawful, and the demonstration yesterday was in clear violation of the law of Canada.
The hon. gentleman who just took his seat berated me for not having rushed out to greet the leaders of the seafarers international union. I would remind him that the leader of that union, and his officers, and the seamen's rights committee had, in a concerted and determined effort, violated the law of Canada and conducted an illegal strike which made it possible for these men to come to Ottawa yesterday.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Would the minister explain what he means by "illegal"? I do not want to interrupt.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
It was a work stoppage clearly in violation of the Canadian labour laws. I think all hon. members ought to bear that in mind in assessing this particular matter.
The president of the seafarers international union did not ask the Minister of Labour, nor to my knowledge any member of the government, for an interview or to be heard in any

particular way. No such request was made yesterday, even though many officers of the union were here. I did, as did other members of parliament, have an opportunity to meet with a large number of the seamen who were here as part of the demonstration and who were electors of the constituency of Inverness-Richmond. I was glad to see them and to spend almost two hours with them in a discussion of this problem. I want to assure my hon. friends in the house that in discharging my responsibilities its impact was made all the more realistic by meeting my own electors and explaining to them the reasons for the trusteeship that had been established by the parliament of Canada.
I found among these men, and among others, misunderstanding about the purpose of the trusteeship and about the possible effect it might have on the union. I assured these men, as I am sure other hon. members did with the seamen they met, that the trusteeship legislation is not intended to destroy the jobs of the seamen. It is intended to protect their jobs.
The legislation is not intended to destroy the seafarers international union as a properly conducted organization. The purpose of the legislation is to strengthen the union by making it more democratic and more effective. The purpose of the legislation is not to carve up the S.I.U. and divide it up among any other unions. The purpose is to make it a proper instrument, serving the union members.
I think many members of the delegation came off their ships through an understandable loyalty to their union rather than through a deep devotion to the leadership of the seafarers international union, because they wanted assurances that their union would not be wrecked. The purpose of the legislation is certainly not in that direction.
In analysing the demonstration yesterday it is apparent that the planning for it was elaborate and conducted in secret. Surely it was obvious, from the directives that had been issued by the committee, that the planning went far beyond the capacity of rank and file members of a trade union. The organization of the demonstration involved the expenditure of funds that required the active and direct participation of the officers, and obviously involved the financial resources of the organization.
It was apparent to all on parliament hill that Mr. Banks had sole and complete authority over what was claimed not to be a strike but a demonstration. It is also significant the men were ordered by him to the hiring halls after the demonstration, but not to the vessels they had left.
Labour Relations
Further, it was apparent many of the men were not aware of the facts in the Norris report. They were unaware of the origin of the report. One seaman suggested to me that the report had been written by the shipping companies, and he sincerely felt it was a document prepared and distributed by the companies in an effort to destroy his union.
There were no incidents. It was a careful, well conducted demonstration, and any of us who know anything about democratic unions must have been surprised at the unanimity and the docility of those union members who appeared on parliament hill yesterday. They were obviously under the direction and leadership of the president and his committee, and were behaving under the specific instructions of this group.
I am also sure that the demonstration revealed there are many men in that union who are not fully behind the present leadership. There were members of that union who came here, not with the enthusiasm that possibly Mr. Banks would like to believe, and this is borne out by the fact that there were many seamen who did not join the demonstration at all. We have been told that the majority of S.I.U. members on the west coast refused to leave their ships, and that there were seamen on ships in various other ports, in central and eastern Canada, who voted against the proposal to go to Ottawa and who later remained on their ships.
I was told this morning that some of the seamen who were in Ottawa yesterday have today drifted back to their jobs. Not all of them have done so, but I feel sure that the great majority of these seamen would prefer to be back at their jobs today. It will indeed be a very sad outcome if these men are ordered to remain away from their work and if further trouble arises, as it is bound to arise, from efforts on the part of shipping companies to man the vessels with other crews. Trouble would come from the kind of conflict arising from such a situation.
It seems to me all of us profoundly wish that these seamen will go back to their work, will obey the law of Canada, and will resume the operations which they were ordered to suspend on Friday last.
On Sunday I sent a telegram to the president of the seafarers international union reminding him that the activity was illegal, and on behalf of the government asking him and his executive officers to obey the law of Canada and to direct all seamen to resume work. On Friday I had made a statement indicating the illegality of this action. On Saturday efforts were made by the Department of Labour to indicate in the strongest and clearest possible terms that this action

Labour Relations
was illegal, and that the men ought to go back to work. On Sunday this was followed up by the telegram to which I have referred, and of course on Monday we had the demonstration.
Today I had an urgent phone call from Mr. Banks. I came out of the cabinet meeting to take this call and Mr. Banks explained why, from his point of view, it was unsuitable for him either to reply to my telegram or for him to meet me yesterday. He then asked to have a meeting with me and said he was prepared to leave his home at once and drive to Ottawa. He wanted such a meeting because he assured me that if I, at a meeting of that kind, asked him or ordered him to send the men back to work, then he at a subsequent meeting with his seamen would be in a much stronger position to influence them in getting them back to work.
I told Mr. Banks I would consider his proposal and call him back. I did so and told him I would see him, provided in the meantime he went before his men and asked them to return to work and to obey the law. I asked him for his assurance that he would make that recommendation to the men, and he gave me that assurance and said he would support it fully. If that happens, if the men are returned to work and if the law is obeyed, I will be glad to see Mr. Banks. If I receive an assurance from Mr. Banks that the men will be asked to obey the law, I will see him. But I am not prepared to meet with Mr. Banks or the officers of the seafarers international union of Canada while the law of Canada is being disobeyed, and while I have received no assurances that every effort has been made by them to see that the law of Canada is complied with.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the minister a question. I am sure he can say what section of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act or the Canada Shipping Act he thinks is in conflict with the seamen coming to Ottawa yesterday under what they claim is a contract condition. Second, what is the difference between this situation and the one where the other seamen asked the shipping companies to allow them to have a day off in order to come to Ottawa yesterday, although not with exactly the same purpose? Why is one illegal, and under what section of the act is it considered to be illegal?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I have not the actual texts before me to enable me to give my hon. friend the precise sections. But there is a provision in the collective agreements between the union and the companies that every consideration

will be given to a seaman who makes a request to go ashore for medical attention, legal counsel or the necessities of life. Consideration is given to such a request. We do not believe this provision of the collective agreements was complied with in the case of seamen who left their ships in violation of this clause and without the permission of the officers or masters of the vessels. In the case of one particular union, I understand that authority was given. In the case of another union it was not given, and this conduct is therefore in violation of the agreement.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Would not this be a matter for grievance procedure between the two parties concerned in the contract, rather than the government declaring it to be an illegal act, which action would, in my opinion, necessitate a definition as to the contravention of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act from the point of view of the federal government. In those circumstances, it would not be a contract dispute between a seaman or a group of seamen and their shipping company.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
This is the point, that any such work stoppage as I have described is a violation of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and is consequently a strike that is unlawful. There is no doubt in the minds of the experienced officers of the Department of Labour that this clearly constitutes an illegal strike. This is the situation.
It seems to me that two weeks ago I was being pressed in this house to end a strike that was fully legal and I withstood pressure in order that the rights of the longshoremen would be fully exercised under the law of Canada. If these men in this situation were out lawfully and in exercise of free collective bargaining, I would take exactly the same attitude as I took with the longshoremen. But in this case I am bound to exercise my responsibility and say that this work stoppage is illegal under the law of Canada, and therefore I am obliged to ask the officers and the seamen to obey the law of Canada. That is the point.

to raise this type of problem. This is what has happened time after time: you say those things but do not do anything.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the help I am receiving from my hon. friend, but I intended to deal with this aspect of the matter. I am not taking any high handed attitude toward the S.I.U. If the officers of the
S.I.U., and Mr. Banks, under the conditions I have described wish to come before the Minister of Labour and discuss the trusteeship legislation, I will attempt to explain to them, as I have explained to seamen, that it will be the desire of the government, as it has been up to this time, to get fair minded men who will be free under the law, without direction from me, to discharge their powers under the act.
I would expect the S.I.U. to be treated fairly and justly under this public trusteeship. It is surely not the intention of parliament that a trusteeship should be set up to inflict injustice upon any individual in Canada, let alone 15,000 members of the S.I.U. That is not the intention. But the law is there and it will be administered by the trustees who will be carrying this heavy responsibility given to them by the parliament of Canada.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Where is Banks going to be?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
As I have stated, the law is there; it has been passed by the parliament of Canada. The trustees will be empowered to exercise that law within the provisions of the act, and it is not my responsibility to prejudge the action of the trustees and to say that any particular man in any particular situation will be dealt with in any way contrary to the provisions declared in the act by the parliament of Canada. I think that is a perfectly proper attitude to take, as minister. No other attitude is consistent with the action taken by the parliament of Canada. This is as I see the situation. I hope I have not been misunderstood with regard to any of the points I have made.
Much has been said about the delays and confusion with respect to the way in which this matter has been dealt with. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in one of his rare flashes of humour described it as a policy of chuckles and postponements. All I can tell him is that in his day we had lots of postponements but very few chuckles. I have no apology to make as to the way we have searched to provide a private trusteeship. I have no apology for that at all, because we did think on two occasions that we were close to agreement. If agreement had been possible, some of the difficulties that we may face in the future might not have arisen. But this was not possible. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the most strenuous and patient
Labour Relations
efforts were made to reach that desirable goal of a private trusteeship, but they failed. There was no other course, then, but to proceed with the legislation, and now to proceed with the selection of the trustees.
Until Sunday there was some last possible hope for the establishment of a private trusteeship and people were negotiating in good faith. Surely while they were negotiating in good faith for a private trusteeship it was not my responsibility to be out looking for public trustees. Surely that would be the wrong thing to do. Now that the private trusteeship has collapsed and there is no possibility of its being agreed upon, the government is searching for public trustees.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we are taking into account the views that have been expressed by members of the House of Commons as to the kind of man required. I am trying to live up to the intimations I gave in the house as to the kind of man that would be asked to serve. I am attempting to carry out those commitments. Just as soon as we have secured the willingness of these men to serve, and they are finally appointed, their names will be announced in the House of Commons. I hope these trustees will command the respect and the confidence of the Canadian people and the respect and confidence of the seamen of Canada whose unions are to be administered by them. Then the act will be proclaimed and the trustees will go about their work. Let me say in conclusion that I hope the trusteeship will secure the support and confidence of the members of the House of Commons and the people of Canada, because it may be that the things that will face the trustees will be very difficult indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Minister of Labour would entertain two questions from me in order to clarify my thinking on these two matters. I do not know what the real reasons are, but if the minister would care to answer I should like to hear from him whether this was the real reason or whether there were other reasons about which we may be hearing later.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: I have one further question on this point. How long a period does the government think is reasonable for this illegal walkout to continue before it undermines the economy of the country?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want anything I say to lead the government or the minister to think that we have changed our views in support of the whole idea of the trusteeship. However, his speech has certainly disturbed me, and some of my colleagues I think, with regard to the analysis he made of the situation. Apparently he has given us a view of what he thinks the mood of the men may be, and their relationships with Hal Banks.
We would like to put the dispute into some kind of time text. It seems to me the reason the situation is crucial at the present time is that the shipping season on the lakes has at the most eight weeks to go. If we have a cold, late November that period may be reduced by as much as two weeks, and we will then have effectively only six weeks more shipping.
We have a very large problem in getting grain to the eastern ocean ports in particular, in order to fill the shipments to Russia which, as everyone agrees, are vital to our economy. With this kind of time sequence of six to eight weeks the time factor is most crucial from the point of view of getting these ships back to work.
All of us in the house, even those who voted against the trusteeship, like the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), have joined in insisting that Hal Banks is a gangster, a crook and a thug. But here we are with the situation where the man led a group of his followers to parliament hill yesterday. It was a well organized demonstration and, with one exception, the members of the S.I.U. to whom I talked expressed deep loyalty to Banks. The man is able to bring this many men here to parliament hill, keep them under good discipline and send them back to where they came from.

This suggests to me and to my colleagues that it is going to take some really sharp and drastic action in order to break the hold that Banks has over these men. I refuse to believe that it is going to be easy for the trusteeship, once it is proclaimed, to step right in and somehow take over. This is why we are concerned. We will all join in the cries about Banks being a thug, a gangster and a criminal, but we have had no legal proceedings or prosecutions against him, either under his immigrant status or as a result of any of the incidents in which he has been involved over such a period of time. It seems almost incomprehensible that the Minister of Labour will now put the onus on the trustees to straighten out what is a crucial timeconsuming situation. That is the only interpretation we can take of his speech, that the onus is now going to lie on the trusteeship working under the authority of the act. I insist that this is not good enough. I think the minister should recognize from his own experience of labour unions that if Banks is not separated from his capacity to control the membership of the S.I.U. we will not get very far.
I should like to report to the house on a conversation I had with one member of the
S.I.U. who came from Port Arthur which I think is as significant as anything the minister reported. This man said: "So Banks is a gangster. So nobody has ever done anything about it. I am worried about my job. There is not much of the season left. Do you think that I or any of my fellows are going to put ourselves out in left field with people like Banks in this kind of situation?" It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this underlines the criticism one might make both of the minister and the government at this time. In this sense we have shifted toward accepting to a degree the kind of criticism which has been expressed in the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), that we have today not been given a really clear picture of how the government intend to move. I insist that the crucial question is: How is the government going to separate Banks and McLaughlin and all these other senior people in the S.I.U. from the capacity or the ability to interfere, and to keep their grip on these men? The press has given one indication of how it can be done; and unless the government has a plan prepared, I think that this situation is likely to lead to some kind of warfare along the docks. This is a suggestion that the C.M.U. is rounding up crews in Montreal and other cities to take over the ships and get the ships moving. If that is done without some attempt 28902-5-246

to sequester Banks and his immediate lieutenants from connection with the men, we will have real warfare on the docks, quite apart from any action taken on the United States side.
I do not want to go on and dot the "i's" of something which has been dotted enough already, but to me the minister's response was most unsatisfactory, particularly to the question put by the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters). Is there no possibility, under any of these statutes of which the minister is in charge, of taking some action against Banks and his lieutenants? Perhaps I am wrong in my impression that the minister will leave it up to the trusteeship, but I suggest that that is going a little too far. I was approached yesterday by a couple of people who asked me what suggestions I would make, and I suggested that one of the things which it seems to me the government must be prepared to do is to have troops, in preference to police, ready to take over the dock facilities during this crucial period of time. That may be necessary. These are the kinds of emergency steps which should be taken, not the dragooning of S.I.U. members, to bring about what we all want, namely, the removal of Banks and his leadership from a situation of control, so that we can get the flow of trade moving again and the trusteeship on its way to doing something with the organization.
If I have misinterpreted the minister and he has an opportunity to clarify the situation, then fine; but I think other hon. members in the house also share my concern at the speech he has made and the interpretation we have been led to put upon it.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) gave us to understand yesterday that the house would be informed today of the government's intentions with respect to this problem of national interest.
This afternoon, the minister concerned stated that he would make a review of the situation and indicate the intentions of the government.
The only thing we learned is that later on a trusteeship will be set up and that trustees will be appointed. He gave us no indication as to whether those trustees have been chosen, whether the negotiations will soon be concluded successfully or whether the trustees will be appointed next week, in ten days or in a month.
He told us also that the strike now going on in Montreal and which threatens to paralyse shipping on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes was absolutely illegal and that union officials had exerted absolutely illegal pressures on union members.
He told us also about the spectacle given for our benefit by union members who, illegally led by their officers, came to Ottawa to demonstrate on the steps of the national parliament itself.
So there we have a cabinet minister who comes and tells us that everything that was done there was absolutely illegal. Yet, when we ask him what he intends to do, all he can say is: tomorrow we might consider the matter.
To make a long story short, this whole speech made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) was only meant to tell us that the situation was just as confused as it was yesterday, the day before, a week ago, two months ago, in short, as it was in August. In short, the situation is only getting worse.
The Minister of Labour told us that he had an announcement to make but he only told us that he was ready to meet Mr. Banks. He even boasted of having talked to him over the telephone. It is surprising how members of the cabinet find it difficult to make telephone calls.
The minister declared that Mr. Banks was guilty of illegal actions. In a word, the only news he could give us today was about the pleasant talk he had with that individual.
In short, this shows how much the situation is confused, and how the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had every reason to assert yesterday that the government did not wish to assume its responsibilities, that it was afraid and according to the Globe and Mail, that it had been waiting during the past three months to find an easy way

out so that it would not lose face. But unfortunately the easy solution is not in view and the situation, instead of improving, is getting worse.
Mr. Speaker, the minister has told us that he is worried. That, in itself, shows a certain progress, even though he was all smiles while making his speech, probably because he wanted once more to have the house and the public believe that there is no need to worry about that problem.
Besides, the minister has told us that it is a trouble which has been existing for a long time and that that type of difficulty is not new, since the previous administrations had to face similar troubles on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish to tell the minister that under the previous government, if we had troubles on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence, we took our responsibilities, and the proof is that it is the predecessor of the present minister who appointed Judge Norris to make a complete investigation into the whole matter of shipping in the great lakes and the St. Lawrence.
If this government postponed the application of the recommendations of the Norris report, I do not think that the minister can throw the blame on the former government for that. Mr. Justice Norris, who is an experienced jurist, did not hesitate to recommend positive action. I do not say that they were easy measures to apply but they were positive, and the government should have assumed its responsibilities at that time.
Today, we hear members from western Canada express their deep concern about our wheat trade with Russia, and about the danger of losing a great part of this famous wheat contract with Russia and other countries behind the iron curtain.
Mr. Speaker, I have just met people living along the St. Lawrence; I come from Three Rivers. And let me tell you that people are greatly worried in that region and have been for a long time. As a matter of fact, the most deplorable acts of violence happened in Three Rivers. They are what prompted the previous government to take action.
Today, the population of Three Rivers, as well as of all the other communities along the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes, have a right to call on the government to assume its responsibilities, act immediately and stop saying that something else will be done tomorrow and the day after.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the St. Lawrence river is the main artery of the economic life of our country. The most beautiful pages of our history were written

on the shores of the St. Lawrence river. That artery is absolutely necessary for the export trade of a country like Canada.
It is really a tragedy that shipping itself on this beautiful waterway should be endangered not only by Mr. Banks and his gang, but also by the delays and indecision of the government.
Let us not forget that Canadian taxpayers have invested millions of dollars in the St. Lawrence river, that the seaway cost about $400 million and that the modernization of the waterway cost approximately $100 million.
It is time the government assumed its responsibilities. The government must not do what it did in the past when it was in power after the war. We then had sea-going merchant ships on which 10,000 Canadian seamen earned a living. Our merchant marine has completely disappeared because the government of the day refused to assume its responsibilities. Even at that time, labour unions were blamed, but nothing was done to put a stop to their wrongdoings. The same thing is happening today. As for us, we proceeded to modernize shipping on the great lakes, and that asset should be preserved for the people of Canada and not wasted simply because the government is afraid of taking its responsibilities with regard to labour unions, which it is first to condemn, but tolerates indirectly.
Today we see irresolution and delay. Mr. Banks was allowed to enter Canada, and now they claim they want to deport him. Sometimes they want to get rid of him, sometimes they wish to keep him there. At any rate, they confirmed his right to stay here as a landed immigrant. And now, they want to take proceedings against him. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) did tell us that he had enlisted the services of two great criminalists in this country in order to launch criminal proceedings against Banks; that happened three months ago and every week since then we have been asking the Minister of Justice to report upon the matter and we always get the same kind of answer from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen): "We shall see tomorrow; tomorrow we shall be in a position to make a statement". The government must come to a decision, and above all they have to decide by themselves what they intend to do.
Indeed, since August, they have been seeking an easy solution. They have turned to the Americans, they have asked the Americans to find an easy solution for them.
One will recall that during the last electoral campaign and since then, these gentlemen have claimed that they were the only ones able to engage in friendly talks with the 28902-5-246J
Labour Relations
U.S. government; they have described how great were the relations of Canada with the United States under the Pearson leadership.
I am not surprised that they rely on the American government for an easy answer. Once more, they are making fools of themselves in the eyes of the Americans, as it happened at least four or five times since this government came to power.
Today, the situation is worse than ever. Canadians complain that their unions are controlled by American unions. That should not be. And what is worse, we have a situation where the union boss, Mr. Meany, together with Mr. Wirtz, a great friend of theirs, treats the sovereign government of this country as if it were a child.
Not only does Mr. Wirtz not co-operate, but he indulges in uncalled for remarks which, I am quite sure, the former government would never have allowed.
The situation is ticklish, it is true; but, after all, it has lasted all of three months. We know that the present government was dead-set against the trusteeship; it has said so on numerous occasions. It has repeatedly postponed the bringing in of this measure in the house, and sought every conceivable means to find a solution which might dispense with such a piece of legislation. What has it achieved in three months?
Do you think that this delay has in any way impressed Mr. Banks? The answer was flaunted in our faces, yesterday, as Mr. Banks paraded with a regal gait on the front steps of parliament. It could be that the trusteeship legislation seemed too drastic to this parliament, and that might be one explanation for the delay.
It would have been possible to find an alternative solution, since they were taking so much time to introduce this trusteeship legislation. If they were afraid of trusteeship, why not come up with something else?
Several of my fellow members of the opposition suggested a secret vote. That suggestion could have proved very useful in this instance. Moreover, a secret vote should be mandatory in all fields under federal jurisdiction. We have seen Judge Lippe insist upon it in the case of the longshoremen's strike. One could not go as far as to say that, if the strike was settled, it was because the vote was secret, but it should be pointed out that the longshoremen did not complain. I honestly believe that if secret ballots were used each time union members are called upon to vote, those union members would be the first to approve such an action.
The government could have required the regular auditing of the seamen's union books

Labour Relations
by a chartered accountant. It could have been done and things could have been straightened out.
If those two solutions had been applied immediately, without even waiting for that trusteeship legislation which the government apprehended, it would have been possible to know if the seamen really wanted Mr. Banks as their leader or if they wanted to prevent the acts of intimidation and mismanagement of which he is accused. It would have been possible to keep him in check if a real auditing of the union's books had been made by a chartered accountant.
The government will be obliged to make a hard decision, it will have to assume its own responsibilities if it wants to impose the trusteeship. But it must be convinced that there is no alternative.
The government must stop relying exclusively on the goodwill of Washington. As stated by the Leader of the Opposition, after all the humiliations and rebuffs the government has suffered in Washington, it should begin to understand that if it wants the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes to be an asset for Canada, and not a liability, it must change its philosophy, especially with regard to the merchant navy.
In my opinion, the government should call a meeting of the labour unions, ship owners, exporters and government representatives to set up a master plan for the long term reorganization of the merchant marine as it was done in France, Switzerland and England. Let us not forget that Canada has today a trade deficit of over $150 million because it does not have a merchant marine.
The setting up of a merchant navy would give employment to about 50,000 Canadians.
The present situation shows how important it is for the government to stop all this beating around the bush and to restore law and order once and for all, within the St. Lawrence maritime unions and in our seaports.
The time has come for the government to prove that it is really willing to act and that it is anxious to restore confidence among Canadians who want law and justice to prevail always.
I do not think that the speech made this afternoon by the Minister of Labour impressed many Canadians in that respect.
Mr. Speaker, the seamen are on the doorstep of parliament and the longshoremen threaten to go back on strike but the Prime Minister is waiting by his telephone, for an easy solution to come once again from Washington.

After all, let us not get too excited over this situation. What we are concerned about, and what everyone seems to be most concerned about, is keeping the ships moving. There is a great deal of sympathy nowadays for communist Russia. People are concerned about keeping the ships moving and keeping wheat flowing to the seaports so that it may be exported. This is well and good, and as an objective is certainly to be commended. After all who is to guarantee, without the calling out of the troops, that if we act without a great deal of consideration these ships are going to continue to move? It must be

remembered that up until Sunday the ships were continuing to move from the head of the lakes to Montreal. After all, this is our objective.
Certainly, we cannot countenance the breaking of the law. However, it must be pointed out that the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), was informed by his department officials that the Canadian seamen's union was breaking the law of Canada as far back as 1959. Why did he not act? The minister refused to act because this labour union belonged to a larger body in the trade union movement, and because they belonged to this larger body this somehow excused their acts of violence and their illegal actions. It appears to be a question of degree. On the one hand, we are prepared to accept these illegal actions because they happen to be committed by a large organization, but now, on the other hand, we are not prepared to accept them because they are committed by a smaller organization. We must take precipitate action. We must accept the Norris report as a court decision and take action immediately. We must deport Mr. Banks or put him in jail.
No legal action has been taken. I think we should face this problem more calmly. I want to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Labour needs no one to speak on his behalf. I am expressing my own opinions as a member of parliament. But none the less I believe I have the right to answer some of the criticism that I have heard here today.
As the opposition have said, there was some delay in introducing the trusteeship legislation, but I think the minister was completely justified in allowing his departmental officers to take considerable time in drafting the legislation, legislation without precedent, so that it would be able to stand up if tested in the courts.

We wanted to make sure that it was in complete conformity with the bill of rights, and that was one reason for the delay.
Since the longshoremen's strike has been brought into this debate I think I should refer to it for a few moments. Here again there was fear and dread expressed by hon. members from the prairie provinces that we were going to lose the sale of a few million bushels of wheat because the long-suffering longshoremen, after negotiating for over a year, had come to the end of the trail and decided to take legal strike action to obtain their just demands. In that incident also the opposition said the government should take immediate action to end the strike. How else does a government take such action except to call in the troops or introduce legislation providing for compulsory arbitration?
Let us be reasonable when we are discussing these matters. We have not lost any sales yet, and I feel quite confident that with the present Minister of Labour we are less likely to lose orders as a result of his improper management of the Department of Labour than at any time over the past six years. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) has suggested a free election in respect to the management of union affairs.
I cannot conceive of any type of election, unless it is secret, being a true democratic election; and the trusteeship legislation provides that in anything which the trustees attempt to foist upon the unions all questions will be decided by a secret ballot, particularly the election of officers.
Nobody need fear anything from this legislation, and now that the opposition has been relatively assured that the government will take the action they have been demanding for the last three months, I notice there is a bit of weakness on their part to support it wholeheartedly. The legislation will be enforced to the letter of the law, but the important factor today is to keep the seamen on the ships. Let us keep the boats moving, at least until freeze-up and they become icebound rather than strike bound.
I met some of the people who took part in yesterday's demonstration. On the one hand we saw that a section of them had fear of

the union leadership, and on the other hand a section appeared to have absolute confidence in that leadership. The ships could be tied up for a longer period if we do not work out some way in which these people will be prepared to accept the trusteeship, in the same manner as it has been accepted by the other four unions involved.
We do not want the ships tied up, and I am sure this is the desire of all hon. members, in addition to cleaning up the S.I.U. I would hope, however, that some of my friends in the far corner of the house do not anticipate that a cleaning up of a union means a changing of its certification. The cleaning up can be done from within, with the help of the trusteeship, but that should not be interpreted as a change of certification.
I appeal to all hon. members to try to keep cool heads. Certainly the minister kept a cool head during the longshoremen's strike, and thus prevented much more serious labour trouble. He is deserving of our confidence. I do not expect members of the opposition to show the same confidence, but at least in the interests of the country's economy let us all pull together and give the minister every support in implementing this legislation, thus assuring that the union will be democratically cleaned up and that the ships can be kept moving until freeze-up.

Mr. Speaker, I had prepared some notes to use when speaking today on this amendment, but after listening to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) would like to scrap those notes and answer the statement made by the minister this afternoon. I think I can safely say that all Canadians would have been rather shocked to hear that statement. I say this with the greatest respect for the minister because I, and I think hon. members generally on this side of the chamber, have great respect for him. We respect him as a gentleman; we respect his method of debating; we respect his oratory. However, I think it was most preposterous that we should hear the Minister of Labour of this country say in his speech that the S.I.U. people, led by Banks, who came here after walking off their ships and leaving their jobs committed an illegal act. When the question was asked as to whether the trusteeship act had been proclaimed, the minister had to admit that it was not the law of Canada; but he also said that according to the statutes of this country which control and govern labour relations, in this situation the march to Ottawa led by Mr. Banks-a recognized friend of the Secretary of State (Mr. 
Pickersgill) of the Liberal government-was illegal. Surely in the face of that statement the whole point is this, that the government of Canada is ready to allow people in this country to break the law. If you take the minister's statement at its worst, it is this: John Jones committed murder, but he only shot one Canadian. We will let him roam around this country and maybe he will not shoot any more Canadians. The minister admitted that we had in this country people who are breaking the law in this regard, but the government is not doing anything to enforce the law of the country.
I listened with a great deal of interest the other evening to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), who said it is always the responsibility of the government to enforce the law and this was the reason he was backing his friends on the other side of the chamber, the Liberal government. I think it is preposterous-and I want to emphasize this again-that this government, believing that the march on Ottawa, the seamen leaving their ships at Canadian docks or ports, or whatever you wish to call them, was illegal is doing nothing to see that the law of this country is enforced.
The Norris report has been handed down since July. In that report was set out the evidence in reference to the lawlessness of Banks and his associates. What stand did the Conservative government take with regard to this matter? I should like to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, whose constituency joins mine in the province of Alberta and whose industry is on all fours with the industry of Bow River. The hon. member stated that the Conservative government had not taken any action in regard to the lawlessness of Banks, his activities, the activities of his union on the great lakes. But the fact is that the Conservative government of that day set up a royal commission to ascertain the facts. You do not try a man without having the evidence; you do not try a man without having the facts, and you do not judge any organization or association in Canada without obtaining the facts.
Mr. Justice Norris held hearings all across this country. He weighed the evidence carefully. There were counsel representing the interested bodies, including the crown, the commission, the unions and various other associations. After weighing that evidence Mr. Justice Norris made certain recommendations. His report was filed in this House of Commons after we had been removed from that side of the house to this side, and the Liberal party formed the government of the day. I say this in answer to the support

given by the Social Credit party-that is, the first Social Credit party, the one led by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), and not the second one. Mr. Speaker, I am not known for making either long speeches or partisan speeches but I should like to beg the indulgence of the house for a few moments because I do not want to let this occasion pass without making a few observations on this important question of trusteeship legislation.
I see little reason for throwing recriminations back and forth from one side of the house to the other. I do not think anybody will come out of this mess with entirely clean hands-neither the former government, nor the government before that, nor the shipping companies with their "sweetheart" deals. I honestly think that despite the speeches we have heard from the other side, most members would agree that the Minister of Labour has done a very good job. I should like to draw attention to one point made this afternoon by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). It was a point which, I thought, brought this whole situation into focus and it concerned the problem raised by Hal Banks. If we say that Hal Banks is the cause of this problem, then, surely, we are saying that either the rank and file of the S.I.U. are his imitators or that there is no communication between the rank and file of the S.I.U.- or of any union, for that matter-and its executive.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) made his point very accurately when he said that we should be concerned, not with this trusteeship legislation, which has already been passed and which must now be carried out, but with the lack of democratic links between the rank and file of the union movement and its executive. The hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out that no one could be expected to have the foolish courage to get up and face Mr. Banks in the open in contradiction to his plans or policies. That stands to reason. I submit we should be concerned in future with legislation to compel the holding of a secret ballot in the election of officers in the union movement. If that were done I think we would have no

Hal Banks, and we would have had no march on Ottawa; because I believe the members of the labour unions are, as you and I, good, honest citizens trying to make a living. I think we should accord to them the opportunity of democratically electing their responsible leadership.
