Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we had a statement from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) in respect of the amendment, and the charges that had been made by the official opposition in that amendment. This statement certainly bore out the facts set out in the amendment, and the charges that are made concerning the actions of this government. This afternoon on orders of the day I asked the minister to answer two questions. The minister said he would be making a statement later and he would then deal with the questions asked of him.
I asked him in respect of a meeting with Mr. Banks and the purpose of that meeting. Well, the minister dealt with that by stating he explained to Mr. Banks in a mild way that he would have a meeting with Mr. Banks provided the S.I.U. members returned to their ships. However, he did not deal in detail with the purpose of the meeting and left that question unanswered. I requested him also to explain the walkout and what the government intended to do with this illegal walkout as the government terms it. The minister did not deal with that at all. He said he hoped that the S.I.U. members would go back to work of their own accord. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have been informed that in Fort William the union voted not to go back to work. Certainly this should precipitate some action on the part of the government to deal with what they term an illegal walkout.
Let us look at the situation that has developed over the period of a few weeks. Negotiations were initiated in respect of a private trusteeship. I would not be surprised if those negotiations were initiated by this government in order to see if they could find a

way out. These negotiations broke down, and we could not find the reason for the breakdown until Mr. Wirtz issued an explanation. The reason for the breakdown was that the C.L.C. insisted on two Canadians being members of the trusteeship, and one person from the United States. It goes without saying, therefore, that the United States must have insisted on two representatives, and one Canadian. This was the reason for the breakdown in negotiations. We had to find this out from the United States rather than from our own government.
Then, the trusteeship bill was introduced because the government could not find any other alternative. All attempts to find an alternative had broken down. The bill was passed unanimously by all parties in this house. Then, after it was passed in the Senate, lo and behold, negotiations for a private trusteeship were resumed. Now I ask, who initiated those negotiations after this House of Commons and the Senate had passed that bill? We have received no answer. There has been delay and evasive answers. Then, over the week end word was received that the negotiations which had been resumed had broken down again.
What was the reason for the breakdown this time? The explanation has been given that they broke down because the S.I.U. membership walked off the boats. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is no explanation at all in my opinion. It is only an excuse. This action by the S.I.U. should have precipitated a private trusteeship. It should have made those who were negotiating more resolved to bring about a trusteeship immediately. The admission was made that Banks had broken the negotiations for a private trusteeship. That is an example of the power this man wields over this government. They cater to his every wish. We would like to be told the real reason for the breakdown of these negotiations, and not the lame excuse that was given by the minister and by others.
This afternoon we had a statement from the minister that the S.I.U. walkout was an illegal walkout. If it was an illegal walkout, why did the government not take some action to get these men back on the ships? Why has there been this delay, this procrastination, these evasive statements that we have been getting in respect of these matters? It is quite clear what action should be taken by the government in this serious situation. The government says, we are going to see what is going to happen; we are going to let somebody else do the job for us. You talk about evasion, procrastination and delay.
Let us take the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) as an example. Special counsel were appointed back in July to look into the Norris

commission report and ascertain what charges might arise from the revelations in that report. They have submitted a report, but no one knows how long ago it was submitted. Questions have been asked in this house for the past three weeks, but the government has treated it as a preliminary report. There has been no action, but somebody in the department is studying it. Then, they have to have another meeting with the two counsellors who were appointed. Is this report so complicated the legal men in the Department of Justice cannot understand it? Why has there been this delay? What is the real reason behind what is happening at this time? What does this report contain? This is what the members of this house want to know and what the people of Canada want to know. Why has the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) laboured so long on this question? Why is the Minister of Justice delaying action on this question? Why is the whole government stalling? What are they waiting for? Are they waiting for things to get so difficult they will have no control over them? Are they waiting for someone else to find a solution? Are they going to telephone to Mr. Wirtz to see if he can settle the problem, just as they asked for his support and his help on previous occasions?
The Minister of Labour says that they are now proceeding to look for trustees. They are looking for trustees after the bill has been passed. Why has there been this delay? Why could they not have had people ready to appoint? They have had all this time since July to find people. In his statement today the Minister of Labour gave credence to the facts outlined in the amendment we introduced, because his statement was one of stalling, of hope, of no action and no trusteeship. There has been nothing but dawdling, delay, inconsistency, confusion, all of which has encouraged chaos and this is the result of the government's fear of making a decision. These are the words in our amendment, and these are the facts as illustrated by what we have seen in the statements we have heard from the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the cabinet. The words of the amendment certainly fit the government's actions, and it is no wonder that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said today they were going to change their minds. Every party in opposition, and indeed hon. members on the other side of the house, ought to support this amendment because deep down in their hearts they know it tells the truth.
We have given the government every opportunity. We have endeavoured to be helpful. We have supported the trusteeship bill; but when the government introduced that bill and said every available means had been

exhausted in attempting to bring about an effective alternative solution to the problem, was it telling the house the truth? Was it just going through the motions? Was it just stalling for time?
The bill was passed, but why has it not been proclaimed? What is the government waiting for-legal advice, or advice from Mr. Banks with respect to this matter? Is that the purpose of the meeting? What is there to discuss with Mr. Banks at this point? Parliament has spoken. The representatives of the people have spoken. The bill has been passed by the other place. All that is needed now is action by the government, this government which told the people of Canada it would give action and direction to the country.
Members of the government gave themselves 60 days, but no action was taken at that time, and many more days have gone by without action. Every day on orders of the day the same answer is given: The government has not yet decided. The people are wondering when the government is going to decide to take action, but indeed the day for action has long past.

Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance to raise tonight which has to do with a subject which I drew to the attention of the treasury benches on October 21 It concerns the manner in which members on the treasury benches are answering the questions which are asked by the opposition.
I thought I would raise the matter tonight because there is more time now for members on the opposition side to voice their views.
I feel, and I believe I am justified in saying so, that while some of the ministers cooperate, the great majority take refuge in equivocation, evasion and vagueness when they are answering questions put to them by members of the opposition. When the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) took part in the discussion on October 21 with relation to the question of privilege I raised he told the house that during the first 70 days of this session some 2,941 questions had been answered as opposed to 1,705 questions in the first 70 days of the last session.
There are two answers to that, Mr. Speaker. The first is that the number of questions which appear on the order paper would not be so large if the ministers of the crown would not equivocate in their answers, but give the direct information to which we feel we are entitled. The second answer to the proposition put by the Secretary of State might well be that the members on this side of the house take their responsibilities a little more conscientiously than the members on the government benches did when they were

in opposition. I have heard hon. members from the Conservative party, the New Democratic party and the two groups in the Social Credit party put question after question to various ministers, yet not once has there been a direct answer.
Today, Mr. Speaker, a question I put concerning the construction of an airport at Mayo was answered by two ministers, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) and the Minister of Northern Affairs, who is not presently in his seat, I am sorry to see. The question was a written one and I asked about the representation being made to the government concerning the construction of an airport at Mayo. The Minister of Northern Affairs said that the only representations he had received were oral, being made to him at the time of his visit this summer to the Yukon. The Minister of Transport was honest enough to say he had received representations as far back as 1962 from myself and others in the Yukon. Why this hiding of information by the Minister of Northern Affairs? Why this hiding of information by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschate-lets) in answer to the question I asked concerning the construction of a minimum security institution in the Yukon? Why cannot we be told when tenders will be called on various projects? Why cannot we have direct and unequivocal answers to the questions we ask? I remember asking the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) a question, which he answered yesterday, concerning consultations which were had with officials of the government of the United States regarding matters of transportation in the Pacific northwest. These matters concerned corridors through to tidewater, the paving of the Alaska highway, the Haines cut-off road, the acquisition of a free port, and so on. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said, as reported on page 3806 of Hansard:
There have been no recent negotiations between the governments of Canada and the United States on any of the five subjects mentioned in the question, although there have been some informal and inconclusive discussions with regard to the Haines cut-off highway.
What did the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) say? Is this one of these snap decisions? He said that the Haines cut-off road would be maintained all year round this winter on a trial basis. Surely this decision was not made between the time the Secretary of State for External Affairs answered the question yesterday and roughly three o'clock this afternoon, when the Minister of National Defence made his announcement, because international negotiations could
Answers to Questions Incomplete not have been carried on in the space of a few hours. This all indicates a serious lack of, for want of a better term, frankness with hon. members of the opposition and the constituencies they represent.

But seriously, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), when speaking to the question of privilege I raised yesterday said, as reported on page 3821 of Hansard:
The hon. member said he could waste the time of the house by asking questions. Surely if his questions are a waste of the time of the house they should not be asked on orders of the day, and they should not be put on the order paper either.
I read these questions which appear on the order paper both when they first appear in Votes and Proceedings and when they appear on the order paper. I read the questions of all hon. members and take an interest in them, and none appear to me to be a waste of time. They are put on the order paper because we do not want to waste the time of the house on orders of the day. We give the government ample opportunity to answer them and plenty of time to come up with some sort of accuracy, truth and unequivocation. But we do not get this. This seems to me to be a dereliction of a duty which ministers who sit on the treasury benches owe to all hon. members. When we take the time and trouble to phrase our questions, the least the government can do is to answer them as fully as they can.
As far as the number of questions is concerned, a point raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that is no criterion at all. While a question placed on the order paper may not have the urgency required for orders of the day, it at least requires the courtesy of a reply. The particular question which raised my point of privilege yesterday was No. 1,272, namely the date on which tenders would be called for the construction of a minimum security penal institution in the Yukon. I asked where the government proposed to construct this institution, and the answer given was: "In the Whitehorse area". The Whitehorse area covers a great deal of ground. The Department of Justice and the Department of Public Works must know precisely where that institution will be constructed, and the least they owe to members on this side is some forthright, frank and truthful information. It was they who assassinated the character of the leader of this party by accusing him of not telling the truth. I ask those who sit now on the treasury benches to practise a little of what they preached over six years.
I need not confine my remarks to questions which are put on the order paper. The questions asked on orders of the day are just as evasively and equivocally answered. We


heard a most shameful display the other day when questions were directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) inquiring as to the whereabouts of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) at a given moment. The right hon. gentleman said, and it is recorded in Hansard that the Minister of Agriculture was in the west attending to the grass roots, or talking to the grass roots, or feeling the grass roots. It was something to do with grass roots-fertilizing them, maybe. Anyway, that was not the truth. It was not the case at all. The minister was not in the west. It seems to me that when such questions are put they deserve an honest and forthright answer.
We heard the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) try to fix the responsibility for a certain document concerning patronage in every constituency in this country. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) denied the existence of such a document, as did the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis). It seems to me it is a denial of the truth and that it makes a farce of the proceedings in this chamber for a minister to say a document does not exist when we see it produced before our very eyes over there in the hands of my hon. friend. Incidentally, it seems passing strange that this million dollar cabinet has to send a $35,000 a year minister out to earn a few bucks at a cattle auction in Ontario.

In fact, it is our duty to work for the general welfare of the country and the ministers should consult the elected members and not other individuals who have no authority in the eyes of the people.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress the views of my constituents in this respect, and if that list is eventually found to be of importance or useful, I will rise again to register my vigorous protests against those dispensers of patronage who have always existed in the past.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want such a situation to arise again in the future, and I hope that the incident will serve as a warning to the hon. minister, until such time as some other irregularity possibly pops up in other departments.

maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on the same grievance. I occasionally put a question on the order paper, so I have had some personal experience of this question. A couple of weeks ago I thought that perhaps all the ministry had had inspiration, since they might have read a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), I believe down in a border city, in which he indicated that what was necessary in this very crucial matter of United States-Canadian relations was an end of platitude-away with platitude, let us have straight talk. At first I thought he had committed himself to an act of self-destruction. I realize, Mr. Speaker, there was perhaps a great awakening here, a great example for the minister.
I should like to think that we could have some straight talk. I can give an example of how lightly the government is answering these questions. My secretary made a mistake in compiling question No. 1,203. I assumed she knew the sex of the person involved, but she did not. So we got this question:
What office does Dallas Taylor hold in the government?
What is his age. place of birth-

And so on. As soon as I saw that, knowing that Dallas Taylor was a female, not a male, I immediately informed the clerk in charge of this.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: You asked her age.

maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Yes, I asked the age. I understood from him that it was changed, but the government puts on the record for all Canada to see that poor Miss Taylor-I think it is "Miss"-is imperishably in print as a male. This is the kind of shoddiness hardly expected of a government.
If shoddiness is not bad enough, I should like to turn to another matter. This is what I would call a flippant reply made to me by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), our house leader, a most august gentleman with a tremendous amount of responsibilities under his wing-and we all appreciate how hard he works at them. This type of answer is the kind of flippancy which really correlates with the arrogance earlier referred to. I asked question No. 1,202, which asked:
What office does Gordon Sheppard hold in the government?
Then it went on to ask what particular qualities of Mr. Sheppard led to his engagement. Part of the answer, as reported on page 3620 of Hansard, was:
In 1961, Mr. Sheppard co-founded Inter-Video Productions Limited to produce television programs and films. From 1961-1963 he was vice president and director of Inter-Video Productions Limited. Included among Mr. Sheppard's television productions was a unique C.T.V. program featuring Mr. Douglas Fisher, M.P.
This is effrontery, Mr. Speaker, when a minister allows an answer which I am sure will be taken by anyone reading it as, in effect, a ridicule of the hon. member involved.
I should like to turn to some other questions I have asked. I asked a question which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) refused to answer on orders of the day. It related clearly to the F.L.Q. I was instructed by you, Mr. Speaker, to put it on the order paper. I put it on as a starred question, and despite the fact that it was elementary in its simplicity it stayed on the order paper for two weeks and into a third week. It asked the Minister of Justice whether the F.L.Q. was considered subversive. I complained about this to a friend of mine, and he replied: "You know the Minister of Justice; he probably thinks you are referring to the federation Liberate in Quebec". But my point is that there is an element of stall.
I would suggest to ministers, if they feel they are giving fair answers, that they examine some of the answers given to me to questions I have put on the order paper relating to the queen's publisher. I have great
Answers to Questions Incomplete suspicions about the operation of that particular department, and have had for several years. It has nothing to do with the incumbent government or the previous government, but with the personnel and set-up there. This concern of mine is evidently shared by some Liberal members, including the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis), who has also placed questions on the order paper. In almost every case where I asked a long series of questions I have been shrugged off or put off with the most evasive and minute of answers. I can remember the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), when he was the conscience of the house in his role as a member of the opposition, making much of the evasiveness of previous ministers. I once remember raising the question of the evasiveness of the Department of Transport when it was headed by Mr. Hees, and as a result of raising that issue I had the satisfaction of an assurance from the minister, and subsequently some good honest and direct answers.
I should like to ask hon. members supporting the government as well as the minister himself, to read some of the answers we have had from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) this year. I ask them, have they really felt we are getting clear and direct answers to the sort of issues we raise? I insist that there is a real element of truth in the charge raised by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), and we will get no better example of it than the kind of answers we have had throughout the session from the Minister of Transport. Lord knows, they are long enough, Mr. Speaker, but they are not clear and almost never relate to the question asked. If the minister wants some specifics I would ask him to look at some of the answers he has given.
One is on the question of run-throughs and the other is on the question of branch line abandonment. Answers of this kind are symptomatic of a government which assumes it will be in power for a long, long time and I think it is a little too early for such an assumption to be made. I should like to compliment some of the ministries whose answers in the main, have been direct. In this regard I can certainly say that in my opinion the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau), and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) have been examples to some of their colleagues. I might say to the President of the Privy Council that, as one of the newer ministers, he might well consider some of the answers he gives which are so short as to be completely noninformative.

I think a serious point has been raised, and if in some parts of my remarks I have allowed levity to creep in I apologize. I am serious as, I think, was the hon. member for Yukon. Already we see an attitude on the part of this government which goes back to days we thought had long gone by. It is almost as if, as one newspaperman put it to me, the events of 1956 and 1957 had not happened.

speechtext:
In the
few minutes which are left of today's sitting I thought that in view of what has taken place this evening it might be appropriate if I were to address myself to the house with reference to what we might expect in the course of the near future. I rise, as I did on another occasion, to say to the government that we on this side of the house, as the official opposition, are prepared to deport ourselves in a way which would do credit, as we have in the past, to the operation of parliament and the entire country.

maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: When are you going to start?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I believe the time to proceed in the proper manner is now. This responsibility is not, in my view, that of the official opposition. I wish the Prime Minister were present this evening. I do not say this in any derogatory way, because I know the function he is attending. I wish he were present because in the light of events I believe the honest and proper course which should be followed now, so that we could present ourselves as a proper parliament to our country without the type of thing which has gone on since the opening of this parliament, should now take place. We should examine the facts; and I do so with trepidation in my heart, because it is not the duty of the whip of any party to rise in the house and make suggestions such as I have in mind this evening. But I am sure they are in the mind of the Prime Minister and of every member of this house. We all find ourselves here as a result of what the electorate has chosen to do. I may think that the electorate in one area might have chosen differently, just as my own views in this regard may be reciprocated. But that is beside the point. We are here in our own right.
I refer to the matter which was raised by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and which was introduced by myself at an earlier date. In fact, it was brought up before that by a member of the New Democratic party. I do not wish to go into specific detail, but I will merely refer to the seriousness of the situation which has developed as a result of the production of this document. On the


day I rose to speak on the subject I quoted Hansard and said at that time that the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis) had misled the house. Because of the fact that I have a great deal of respect for the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill)-I think he is aware of this-I said the Postmaster General had also misled the Secretary of State.
Then we had a situation where the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh) was participating in provincial matters. This was a gross error as far as the rights of the provinces are concerned.

speechtext: I have two minutes. After I have finished I will certainly allow the hon. lady to ask her question.

speechtext: I think that since the hon. gentleman has changed the subject I have the right to rise on a question of privilege. I should only be a second. The Postmaster General did not mislead me in any way, nor did I mislead the house. If the hon. gentleman will read the motion which was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) he will find that the motion is extremely clear and specific. It refers to a document prepared by the Postmaster General-

speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The hon. member raised a question affecting my personal reputation. He did it very nicely but, surely, since he suggested I was led into misleading the house I should be permitted to put the facts briefly on record.

maintopic: COMPLAINT ALLEGING INCOMPLETE ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the house will not be surprised when I rise to remind you that the Secretary of State has once again risen to take part in a discussion without being formally recognized. There may have been a nod from you, but I did not see it. May I recall that one of my hon. friends rose six or seven times earlier today in an attempt to catch your eye on a question of privilege, but failed to do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

May I continue in the one minute left to me? I will terminate at the end of that time. I will continue by referring to the Minister of Agriculture along the same lines as were pursued by my hon. friend from Yukon. I do not say for one moment that the Prime Minister misled the house, because I do not think that would be a fair thing to say; but certainly, then, the Minister of Agriculture misled the Prime Minister in the statement he made today. There is an old phrase, possibly shopworn, which runs: "There is a tide in the affairs of men which, taken at

the flood, leads on to fortune." The fortune is ours, as Canadians. The responsibility that lies upon us is to discharge the business of this country and I believe the most important task which faces the Prime Minister tonight is to ask for the resignation of the three ministers to whom I have referred.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the house leader, Mr. Speaker, if the order of business as outlined yesterday holds for tomorrow, Thursday and Friday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, with one slight exception, sir. The Prime Minister has reminded me that he had begun to speak on a motion to set up a committee on procedure, and suggested to me that before we embark on the income tax bill again we should complete that debate, which I think there was some disposition to feel could be done fairly quickly.
